questionsToConsider: Which fabrics and duvet weights do you stock, and which result should each one sit under?
Do you sell deep-pocket fitted sheets, and at what mattress depth should you suggest them?
Should allergy answers lead to specific products, such as synthetic fillings instead of down?
Would a colour or pattern question help, or is that better left to the product page?
guide.howToUseResponses: Use the bed size and mattress depth to check that the set you recommend actually fits before the customer orders, which saves a lot of returns. The allergy answers tell you when to steer someone away from feather and down fillings. Over time, the split between cool, all-season and cosy results is a useful guide for how much of each fabric to stock by season.
customizeSteps: Rename each result after the collection it matches in your store and describe what's in it.
Check the scores on the four warmth questions and move the bands if your range has more than three warmth levels.
Embed the quiz on your bedding category page or link to it from product pages where shoppers get stuck.

faqs.q: How do I choose the right bedding for how I sleep?
faqs.a: Start with temperature. Hot sleepers do best with breathable percale or linen and a light duvet, cold sleepers with brushed cotton or flannel and a heavier one.

faqs.q: What is the difference between percale and sateen sheets?
faqs.a: Percale has a crisp, matte, cool feel. Sateen has a smoother, silkier surface with a slight sheen and feels a little warmer.

faqs.q: Why does the quiz ask about mattress depth?
faqs.a: Fitted sheets come with different pocket depths, and a deep mattress or topper can pull a standard sheet off the corners. Knowing the depth lets you recommend a sheet that stays put.

faqs.q: How are the bedding results worked out?
faqs.a: Four questions about sleep temperature, room, feel and season each add points to a warmth score. The total picks cool, all-season or cosy bedding, and you can edit the points and bands.

endings.title: Cool and breathable ❄️
endings.bodyMd: Cotton percale or linen with a lightweight duvet. Percale is crisp and matte, and linen gets softer with every wash; both breathe well, which is what a hot sleeper needs. If you'd rather not iron, linen looks good a little rumpled.

endings.title: Warm and cosy 🧣
endings.bodyMd: Brushed cotton or flannel sheets with a heavier winter duvet. Brushed cotton traps a little warmth and feels soft from the first night, which is exactly what a cold sleeper in a chilly room wants.

endings.title: Cotton sateen, all season 🛏️
endings.bodyMd: Smooth cotton sateen sheets with a medium-weight duvet. Sateen feels silky and a touch warmer than crisp cotton, so it works across the year without swapping sets each season.
